blocks.text: A) Imagine a drug that could enhance a child's creativity and critical thinking. Imagine that this drug were simple to make, safe to take, and could be had for free. The nation's leading pediatricians (儿科医生) say this miracle compound exists. In a new clinical report, they are urging doctors to prescribe it liberally to the children in their care.

blocks.text: B) "This may seem old-fashioned, but there are skills to be learned when kids aren't told what to do," said Dr. Michael Yogman, a Harvard Medical School pediatrician who led the drafting of the call to arms. blocks.text: C) The advice, issued Monday by the American Academy of Pediatrics, may come as a shock to some parents. After spending years fretting (烦恼) over which toys to buy, which apps to download and which skill-building programs to send their kids to after school, letting them simply play-or better yet, playing with them-could seem like a step backward. The pediatricians insist that it's not. The academy's guidance does not include specific recommendations for the dosing of play. Instead, it asks doctors to advise parents before their babies turn two that play is essential to healthy development.

blocks.text: D) "Play is not silly behavior," the academy's report declares. It fosters children's creativity, cooperation, and problem-solving skills-all of which are critical for a 2lst-century workforce. When parents engage in play with their children, it builds a wall against the harmful effects of all kinds of stress, including poverty, the academy says. In the pediatricians' view, essentially every life skill that's valued in adults can be built up with play. "Collaboration, negotiation, decision-making, creativity, leadership, and increased physical activity are just some of the skills and benefits children gain through play," they wrote. The pediatricians' appeal comes as kids are being squeezed by increasing academic demands at school and the constant invasion of digital media.

37. Since the beginning of this century, an increasing amount of time has been shifted in public schools from recess to academic activities.
38. It has been acknowledged that while kids may welcome pediatricians' recommendation, their parents may doubt its feasibility.
39. According to some professionals, deprivation of young children's playtime will do harm not only to children themselves but to the country and the world.
40. By playing with children, parents can prevent them from being harmed by stress.
41. Playing with digital devices discourages kids from active discovery, according to pediatrician
42. The suggestion of letting children simply play may sound like going backwards to parents who want to help build their children's skills.
43. Dr. Michael Yogman believes the idea that parents should carefully schedule children's time may not be helpful to their growth.
44. One quarter of teachers in an American city said that children in kindergartens had no time for playing freely.
45. According to a pediatrician, no matter what kind of play children engage in, they are learning how to create things.
46. What does the author say may have an adverse impact on people?

options.label: A.
options.text: Undergoing plastic surgeries in pursuit of beauty.

options.label: B.
options.text: Imitating the lifestyles of heroes and role models.

options.label: C.
options.text: Striving to achieve perfection regardless of financial cost.

options.label: D.
options.text: Attempting to meet society's expectation of appearance.

questions.stem: 47. What have researchers found out about people's earnings?

options.label: A.
options.text: They are closely related to people's social status.

options.label: B.
options.text: They have to do with people's body weight and shape.

options.label: C.
options.text: They seem to matter much less to men than to women.

options.label: D.
options.text: They may not be equal to people's contributions.

questions.stem: 48. What does the author's recent study focus on?

options.label: A.
options.text: Previous literature on indicators of competitiveness in the workplace.

options.label: B.
options.text: Traits that matter most in one's pursuit of success in the labor market.

options.label: C.
options.text: Whether self-perception of body image impacts one's workplace success.

options.label: D.
options.text: How bosses' perception of body image impacts employees' advancement.

questions.stem: 49. What is the finding of the author's recent research?

options.label: A.
options.text: Being overweight actually does not do much harm to the overall well-being of employees.

options.label: B.
options.text: People are not adversely affected in the workplace by false self-perception of body weight.

options.label: C.
options.text: Self-esteem helps to combat gender inequality in the workplace.

options.label: D.
options.text: Gender inequality continues to frustrate a lot of female employees.

options.text: Banning discrimination on the basis of employees' body image.

options.label: B.
options.text: Expanding protection of women against gender discrimination.

options.label: C.
options.text: Helping employees change their own perception of beauty.

options.label: D.
options.text: Excluding body shape as a category in the labor contract.

options.text: The hope of achieving a thriving life is impossible to realize.
